title: Drawing logical conclusions
blurb: Combine a passage's details into the conclusion it best supports, and reject conclusions that claim more than the evidence shows.
question: A HESI A2 passage says a clinic added Saturday hours, most Saturday visitors turned out to be existing patients, and weekend emergency room visits by its patients fell by nearly a third. The question asks which conclusion is best supported. Why is 'Saturday hours were a failure' wrong, and what makes the right answer right?

teach.body: Formally, a conclusion is a judgment reached by combining details in a text; it must be consistent with all of the relevant details and contradict none of them. HESI A2 stems read 'Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?' or 'Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree that...'. In plain English: a conclusion is what the facts add up to, and the best one claims no more than the facts can carry.

(1) When Riverside Clinic began opening on Saturday mornings, managers expected the extra hours to attract new patients. Instead, most Saturday visitors were existing patients who used to go to the emergency room for minor problems on weekends.

(2) Clinic records show that weekend emergency room visits by its patients fell by nearly a third. The extra shift cost more in staff wages than managers had planned. Even so, the board voted in January to keep Saturday hours for another year.

root.label: Riverside passage
root.sub: What do the details add up to?

teach.caption: Each conclusion is backed by the text and clashes with nothing. 'It saved money' or 'it failed' is not.

items: Read the stem: is it about the whole passage or one paragraph?
Sum up what the details add up to in a few words before reading the options.
Clash check: look for any sentence that contradicts the option; one clash eliminates it.
Strength check: does the option claim more (all, proves, caused, will) than the details show?
Choose the most modest option that still uses the evidence.

teach.caption: An overreach is not contradicted; it simply goes past what the passage shows.

teach.h: A conclusion must fit every detail
teach.body: Test a conclusion against the whole passage, not one sentence. 'The board ended Saturday hours because they cost too much' fits the cost detail but contradicts the January vote, so it fails. 'Saturday hours were a failure' ignores the drop in emergency room visits. The best-supported conclusion is the one that is most strongly backed by the text and clashes with nothing in it.

bands.label: Must be true or strongly supported
Possible, but the text is silent

teach.caption: On the HESI A2, 'could be true' is not enough. Choose the option the text backs most strongly.

teach.text: Three classic conclusion traps: (1) overgeneralization, from one clinic, one study or one group to everyone; (2) a cause claimed from details that only show two things happened at the same time; (3) a view the author reports ('critics argue...') taken as the author's own conclusion. Words such as 'proves', 'all' and 'caused' need equally strong support.

teach.body: Jasmine Okafor, applying to a BSN program, reads the Riverside passage and the stem 'Which conclusion is best supported?' She rejects 'Saturday hours lost money for the clinic' because the passage says wages were higher than planned, not that the clinic lost money. She rejects 'Saturday hours will soon draw many new patients' because the passage reports the opposite so far. She picks 'Saturday hours cut weekend emergency room visits by the clinic's patients,' which the records back and nothing contradicts.

steps.label: Add up the details
steps.sub: Say the gist in a few words

items: A conclusion combines details and must contradict none of them.
The best answer is the most modest option that still uses the evidence.
Respect the numbers: 'fell by a third' is not 'most stopped'.
Two things happening together do not prove that one caused the other.
A view the author only reports is not the author's conclusion.

summary: You can now draw the conclusion a passage best supports by testing each option against every detail and every number it gives. You can also reject overgeneralizations, causes claimed from mere timing, and views the author only reports.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Last fall, Grant High School moved its first bell from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. By spring, first-period absences had dropped by about 20 percent, and the number of students marked late fell even more. Some coaches warned that practices would end too late in the evening, yet the number of students signing up for sports teams stayed about the same as the year before.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The later bell improved attendance without lowering sports sign-ups.
The later bell raised student grades in most subjects by the spring.
Coaches persuaded the school to shorten its practices after the change.
Students slept about an hour longer each night after the later bell.
A.why: The passage reports fewer absences and fewer late students, and says sports sign-ups stayed about the same. The conclusion combines both details and goes no further.

whyNot.1: Grades are not mentioned; this conclusion has no support in the text.
whyNot.2: The coaches raised a concern, but the passage does not say practices were shortened.
whyNot.3: This may seem likely from outside knowledge, but the passage gives no sleep data.

A.q:
Read the passage.

The Maplewood Public Library began lending free reading glasses at its front desk in March. Staff had noticed patrons squinting at forms and newspapers. By June, the desk had lent glasses more than 600 times. Several patrons said they had been embarrassed to ask for help before. The library buys the glasses in bulk for about two dollars a pair.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Most library patrons need reading glasses to read forms and newspapers.
The library spends more on glasses than on any other service it offers.
Patrons stopped asking staff for any help once the glasses were offered.
The glasses program met a need that patrons had been reluctant to voice.
A.why: More than 600 loans in about three months shows real demand, and patrons said they had been embarrassed to ask for help. Together these support a need patrons had been reluctant to voice.

whyNot.0: Overgeneralization: 600 loans shows many patrons used the glasses, not that most patrons need them.
whyNot.1: The glasses cost about two dollars a pair; the passage does not compare this with other services.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: patrons said they had been embarrassed to ask before; the passage does not say they stopped asking for other help.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Desmond took the bus to his nursing clinicals for the first month of the term. In October he began leaving home 40 minutes earlier, and his instructor noted that he had not been late once since. He told a classmate the earlier bus was less crowded, so he could review his notes on the ride.

Which conclusion is consistent with ALL of the details in the passage?
options: Desmond stopped taking the bus and began driving in October.
Desmond's change in routine helped both his timing and his study.
Desmond's instructor required him to arrive 40 minutes early.
Desmond was late to every clinical shift during the first month.
A.why: He has not been late since October, and the quieter bus lets him review notes. A conclusion covering both effects fits every detail.

whyNot.0: This contradicts the passage: he still takes a bus, just an earlier one.
whyNot.2: The instructor noted his punctuality; the passage does not say the instructor required the change.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: the passage implies he was sometimes late before, not late every time.

B.q:
Read the passage.

A hospital replaced the overhead paging system on two units with silent pagers that vibrate on each nurse's badge. On those units, nurses reported fewer interruptions during medication rounds. Patients' scores for 'quiet at night' rose from 61 to 78 percent over six months. On units that kept overhead paging, the same score barely changed.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The silent pagers most likely made the two units quieter at night.
Nurses on the two units answered pages more slowly than before.
Overhead paging was removed from every unit in the hospital.
Patients on all units rated the hospital quieter after six months.
B.why: Quiet scores rose sharply on the units with silent pagers and barely changed on units that kept overhead paging. That comparison points to the pagers rather than a hospital-wide change, and 'most likely' keeps the claim modest.

whyNot.1: Response times are not mentioned; nurses reported fewer interruptions, which is a different point.
whyNot.2: Contradicts the passage: some units kept overhead paging.
whyNot.3: Contradicts the passage: the score barely changed on units that kept overhead paging.

B.q:
Read the passage.

At Sunnyvale Elementary, the school nurse began sending home a one-page sheet on handwashing with every student who visited her office with a cold. Over the winter, her office logged 15 percent fewer visits for colds than the winter before. Parents of three students called to say the sheet was helpful.

Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The handwashing sheets ended the spread of colds at the school.
Most parents at Sunnyvale found the sheet helpful and read it.
Cold-related visits fell in the winter after the sheets went out.
The handwashing sheets caused the drop in visits for colds.
B.why: The text states that visits for colds fell 15 percent the winter the sheets were sent. That is directly supported; claims about cause or about most parents go further than the evidence.

whyNot.0: Overstatement: visits fell by 15 percent; colds did not stop spreading.
whyNot.1: Three phone calls cannot show what most parents thought.
whyNot.3: The passage shows the drop came after the sheets, not that the sheets caused it; other factors are not ruled out.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Carla Ruiz has volunteered at the county food bank every Saturday for six years. She began by stacking cans in the warehouse. Two years ago she started training new volunteers. Last spring the director asked her to design the food bank's new delivery routes. Carla says she still enjoys the quiet of the warehouse most.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Carla prefers training volunteers to designing delivery routes.
Carla's responsibilities at the food bank have grown over time.
Carla plans to leave the warehouse for a paid job as director.
The food bank's director trains every new volunteer personally.
B.why: She moved from stacking cans to training volunteers to designing delivery routes at the director's request. Together these details show her responsibilities growing over six years.

whyNot.0: Unsupported: the only preference she states is for the quiet of the warehouse.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage mentions no plans to leave or to take a paid job.
whyNot.3: Contradicts the passage: Carla trains new volunteers.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The town of Elm Ridge offered free smoke alarm installation to every household in 2023. Firefighters installed alarms in about 1,200 homes, mostly in older neighborhoods. In 2024, the town had the same number of house fires as in 2022, but no one died in a house fire in 2024, compared with three deaths in 2022.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The program reduced the number of house fires in older areas.
Fire deaths fell after the program, though fires did not decline.
Every household in Elm Ridge received a free alarm during 2023.
Older neighborhoods had more fires than newer ones in 2024.
C.why: The passage gives the same number of fires in both years but zero deaths in 2024 versus three in 2022. The conclusion matches both facts and claims no more.

whyNot.0: This contradicts the passage: the number of house fires stayed the same.
whyNot.2: The offer went to every household, but alarms were installed in about 1,200 homes; the text does not say all accepted.
whyNot.3: The passage does not compare fire counts by neighborhood.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Pharmacist Lena Kowalski noticed that many older customers returned with questions about new prescriptions. She began spending two minutes with each first-time prescription, explaining the dose and showing the label. Over the next three months, return visits with questions fell by half, and the line at her counter grew slightly longer at peak hours. She has kept the practice ever since.

Based on the passage, Lena would most likely agree that:
options: a longer line at peak hours outweighs fewer return visits
every customer should get ten minutes with the pharmacist
unclear labels are the main reason customers come back
a short talk at pickup is worth a slightly longer line
C.why: Return visits fell by half while the line grew only slightly, and she has kept the practice. Her choice shows she judges the short talk worth the small cost in waiting time.

whyNot.0: Reverses her judgment: she kept the practice despite the longer line, so she values the fewer return visits more.
whyNot.1: Overreach: she spends about two minutes, and only with first-time prescriptions.
whyNot.2: Unsupported cause: she explains the dose and shows the label, but the passage does not blame unclear labels for return visits.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Three community gardens opened in Fairview last year. At the Oak Street garden, neighbors who had never met now share tools and recipes. At the Pine Avenue garden, retirees teach teenagers how to plant tomatoes. At the Lake Road garden, families organized a harvest supper that drew 80 people.

Which conclusion is best supported by the examples in the passage?
options: Fairview's gardens have brought residents together.
Fairview's gardens produce most of the town's food.
Fairview's retirees enjoy gardening more than others.
Fairview should open a garden in each neighborhood.
C.why: Each example shows people connecting: neighbors sharing, retirees teaching teenagers, families hosting a supper. The conclusion generalizes what all three have in common.

whyNot.1: Food production for the town is not measured or mentioned.
whyNot.2: Retirees appear in one example; the passage compares no groups' enjoyment.
whyNot.3: This is a recommendation the author does not make; the passage describes, it does not propose.

reteach.title: Think like a detective
reteach.question: A detective announces, 'The butler did it.' Before agreeing, the judge checks that claim against every clue in the case. How is that like answering a HESI A2 conclusion question?

blocks.h: One clue that does not fit sinks the case
blocks.body: A detective's conclusion must explain every clue and must not claim more than the clues show. If the butler was in the house but the muddy boots by the garden door are two sizes too big for him, 'the butler did it' fails. 'Someone came in from the garden and walked to the kitchen' fits every clue and claims no more. HESI A2 conclusion items work the same way: test each option against every detail, and prefer the one that stays inside the evidence.

blocks.text: A conclusion that fits most of the clues is still wrong if one clue contradicts it. Check every paragraph before you commit.

explain.body: A conclusion is a judgment you reach by combining details. It must agree with every relevant detail and contradict none. If one sentence in the passage clashes with it, it is wrong, however reasonable it sounds.

test.q:
Read the passage.

After a city added bike lanes on Main Street, bike counts there doubled in a year. Shop owners on the street reported steady sales, and the number of crashes involving cyclists stayed about the same.

Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Cycling on Main Street grew without hurting local shop sales.
The bike lanes made Main Street much safer for every cyclist.
Shop owners on Main Street opposed the lanes before they opened.
Most residents of the city now ride bikes to work on Main Street.
test.why: Bike counts doubled and sales held steady: the conclusion combines both details and contradicts none.

whyNot.1: Crashes stayed about the same, so 'much safer' is not supported.
whyNot.2: The passage gives no information on what shop owners thought beforehand.
whyNot.3: Doubled bike counts on one street say nothing about most residents' commutes.

explain.body: Numbers limit what you may conclude. A 20 percent drop is not 'most stopped', 'about a third' is not 'half', and a figure for one group or one year does not cover another. Check the size, the group and the time of every number an option uses.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Our town's new walking trail opened in May. It follows the old rail line for three miles, and volunteers planted 200 native shrubs along the route.

(2) A counter at the trailhead recorded 9,000 visits in the first summer. In the second summer, the counter recorded 7,500 visits, and the town added benches every half mile.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Most residents stopped using the trail in its second summer.
The trail lost about half of its visitors in its second summer.
Trail visits were lower in the second summer than in the first.
Visits fell because the town did not maintain the trail well.
test.why: The counter shows 9,000 visits the first summer and 7,500 the second: visits were lower. The drop of 1,500 is about one sixth, so stronger claims overstate it.

whyNot.0: Overstatement: 7,500 visits is still most of the first summer's total, not a collapse in use.
whyNot.1: Number slip: 1,500 fewer visits out of 9,000 is about 17 percent, not half.
whyNot.3: Unsupported cause: the passage gives no reason for the drop and even mentions new benches.

explain.h: Together is not the same as because
explain.body: Many options could be true in real life. The right answer is the one the text supports most strongly. When two changes happen at once, or a result simply follows a change, the passage shows timing, not cause. 'Fell after' is supported; 'was caused by' usually is not.

test.q:
Read the passage.

A dental office began texting reminders two days before appointments. That year, missed appointments fell from about 12 percent to 7 percent. The office also hired a second receptionist in the same year.

Which conclusion is most strongly supported?
options: The text reminders caused the drop in missed appointments.
Missed appointments fell in the year the reminders began.
The new receptionist reduced missed appointments by half.
Patients prefer text reminders to phone calls from staff.
test.why: The text directly shows missed appointments fell in the same year reminders started. Because a receptionist was also hired, it cannot show which change caused the drop.

whyNot.0: Two changes happened that year, so the text cannot pin the cause on the reminders.
whyNot.2: The passage does not credit the receptionist, and 12 to 7 percent is not a drop by half.

explain.h: The author's view vs a reported view
explain.body: Passages often report what others think ('some parents worry', 'critics argue') and then answer it. The author's conclusion comes from the author's own evidence and wording, not from a view the author reports in order to answer it.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Some parents worry that a later start time for middle school will simply push bedtimes later. (2) When Pine Valley Middle School moved its first bell from 7:40 to 8:30, researchers surveyed students before and after the change. Bedtimes moved about ten minutes later, but wake times moved nearly forty minutes later, so students averaged about half an hour more sleep on school nights.

Which conclusion would the author most likely agree with?
options: Later start times push bedtimes back by about the same amount.
Every middle school should start its first class at 8:30 a.m.
Pine Valley's later start gave students more sleep on school nights.
Students at Pine Valley now get the sleep that doctors recommend.
test.why: The survey the author cites shows bedtimes moved ten minutes while wake times moved forty, for about half an hour more sleep. That is the author's evidence-based conclusion.

whyNot.0: This is the parents' worry that the author reports and then answers with the survey; bedtimes moved only ten minutes.
whyNot.1: Overgeneralization: the passage describes one school and makes no recommendation for every school.
whyNot.3: Outside knowledge: the passage does not say how much sleep doctors recommend.
